title: The first computer mouse was a wooden block rolling on two metal wheels

cover.alt: Douglas Engelbart's prototype mouse, a small wooden box with a button and a cord, in a museum display beside an early Logitech prototype.

body: [Douglas Engelbart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Engelbart) and his engineer Bill English built the first mouse at the Stanford Research Institute in the mid-1960s: a **wooden shell** over two metal wheels set at right angles, each turning a potentiometer, so that sliding the block sideways turned one wheel and pushing it forward turned the other. Engelbart said the nickname came from the cord trailing out of the end like a tail. He showed it to the public on 9 December 1968 in the presentation now called the Mother of All Demos, alongside hypertext and on-screen collaboration. SRI held the patent, granted in 1970, and later licensed it to Apple for what Engelbart recalled as "something like $40,000"; it expired before mice became common on personal computers, and he never received royalties.

slides.alt: The underside of a replica of Engelbart's mouse, showing two metal wheels mounted at right angles to each other.
slides.caption: The underside of a replica of the mouse Douglas Engelbart's team built at the Stanford Research Institute (SRI): two wheels at right angles, one for each direction of movement.

slides.prompt: SRI licensed the mouse patent to Apple. For roughly how much, according to Engelbart?
slides.detail: Engelbart said SRI "really had no idea of its value". The patent, US 3,541,541, expired before mice became common on personal computers, so he never earned royalties.

left.label: Myth
left.text: Apple invented the mouse for the Macintosh in 1984.

right.label: Fact
right.text: Engelbart and engineer Bill English built it at SRI in the 1960s. Xerox's Alto used one in 1973; the Macintosh of 1984 helped make it ordinary.

events.text: Xerox Alto comes with a mouse

slides.question: Why did Engelbart earn nothing from the mouse?
options: SRI owned the patent; it expired early
He gave the rights to Xerox
He sold the idea for one dollar
slides.explanation: The patent belonged to SRI, his employer, and it ran out before mice became common on personal computers, so there were no royalties to collect.
